stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: prove financially successful for some musicians but disappointing for others.
choices.B: hold greater financial appeal for bands than for individual musicians.
choices.C: cause most musicians who use the model to lower the suggested prices of their songs and albums over time.
choices.D: more strongly reflect differences in certain musicians’ popularity than traditional pricing models do.

explanation: Harvey Danger earned less than hoped, with only about 1% paying; Siberry did well because listeners paid above the suggested price. Two opposite outcomes from the same model. B and D introduce band-versus-solo and popularity comparisons the examples don't establish.

passage.t: One theory behind human bipedalism speculates that it originated in a mostly ground-based ancestor that practiced four- legged “knuckle-walking,” like chimpanzees and gorillas do today, and eventually evolved into moving upright on two legs. But recently, researchers observed orangutans, another relative of humans, standing on two legs on tree branches and using their arms for balance while they reached for fruits. These observations may suggest that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: bipedalism evolved because it was advantageous to a tree-dwelling ancestor of humans.
choices.B: bipedalism must have evolved simultaneously with knuckle-walking and tree-climbing.
choices.C: moving between the ground and the trees would have been difficult without bipedalism.
choices.D: a knuckle-walking human ancestor could have easily moved bipedally in trees.

explanation: Orangutans stand on two legs in trees and use their arms for balance while reaching for fruit. That's an alternative to the knuckle-walking story: bipedalism could have paid off up in the branches. D keeps the knuckle-walking ancestor the observations were offered against.

passage.t: Arthur Conan Doyle’s stories about detective Sherlock Holmes were published between 1887 and 1927. They have inspired countless successful adaptations, including comic strips, movies, and a television series Sherlock Hound, directed by Hayao Miyazaki, who is celebrated for his animated movies. Until 2014, these stories were copyrighted. The right to adapt was only available to those who could afford the copyright fee and gain approval from the strict copyright holders of Doyle’s estate. Some journalists predict that the number of Sherlock Holmes adaptations is likely to increase since the end of copyright means that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: Doyle’s original stories will become hard to find.
choices.B: people will become more interested in detective stories than they were in the 1800s.
choices.C: producing adaptations will become easier and less expensive.
choices.D: the former copyright holders of Doyle’s estate will return fees they collected.

explanation: While the stories were copyrighted, adapting them meant paying a fee and getting approval from a strict estate. Once copyright ends, both obstacles go, so adaptations get cheaper and easier — which is why more are predicted.

passage.t: Songbirds learn to respond to and imitate their species’ songs from an early age. With each generation, small differences are introduced that result in distinct variations—called dialects—among geographically isolated populations of the same species. A research study examined whether twelve-day-old Ficedula hypoleuca (pied flycatcher) nestlings prefer local dialects over the unfamiliar dialects of nonlocal F. hypoleuca populations: the more begging calls the nestlings made in response to a song, the stronger their preference. The researchers found that nestlings produced more begging calls in response to their own dialect than to nonlocal dialects. Since song preference plays a role in songbird mate selection, the finding suggests that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: F. hypoleuca nestlings’ preference for their own dialect likely disappears as they mature to promote socialization between different F. hypoleuca populations.
choices.B: F. hypoleuca nestlings who show an early preference for their own dialect are likely to receive more food from their caretakers than nestlings who show no preferences among any F. hypoleuca dialects.
choices.C: F. hypoleuca nestlings’ preference for their own dialect likely drives them when they mature to reproduce with other F. hypoleuca from local rather than nonlocal populations.
choices.D: F. hypoleuca nestlings show a preference for both local F. hypoleuca dialects and the songs of other local songbirds over the songs of nonlocal birds of any species.

explanation: Nestlings begged more at their own dialect, and song preference feeds into mate selection. Carried forward, that means grown birds should favour mates from their own local population. A has the preference disappearing, which would break the link the question draws.

passage.t: One challenge when researching whether holding elected office changes a person’s behavior is the problem of ensuring that the experiment has an appropriate control group. To reveal the effect of holding office, researchers must compare people who hold elected office with people who do not hold office but who are otherwise similar to the office-holders. Since researchers are unable to control which politicians win elections, they therefore ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: struggle to find valid data about the behavior of politicians who do not currently hold office.
choices.B: can only conduct valid studies with people who have previously held office rather than people who presently hold office.
choices.C: should select a control group of people who differ from office holders in several significant ways.
choices.D: will find it difficult to identify a group of people who can function as an appropriate control group for their studies.

explanation: A control group must match office-holders in every way except holding office, and researchers can't decide who wins elections. So assembling that comparison group is the difficulty. C recommends a group that differs in several ways, which defeats the purpose.

passage.t: One aspect of in-person shopping that online shopping can’t replicate is the opportunity to touch a product before buying it. Does this difference matter? In an experiment, researchers asked one group of participants to touch a mug and a toy, while another group was prohibited from touching the two items. The participants were then asked how much money they’d pay for the items. People who got to touch the items were willing to pay much more money for them than were people who weren’t allowed to touch the items. This finding suggests that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: people who mainly shop online probably spend more money every month than people who mainly shop in person do.
choices.B: in-person shopping may make products seem more valuable than they seem if only viewed online.
choices.C: retailers with in-person and online stores should charge the same price for a given product in both places.
choices.D: online retailers may be able to raise the prices they charge for products that are only available online.

explanation: People allowed to touch the mug and toy would pay more than those who couldn't. Since touching is what in-person shopping adds, handling a product makes it seem worth more. D applies the finding to online-only goods, where no touching occurs.

passage.t: German theater practitioner Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) believed that theater should elicit an intellectual rather than an emotional response from audiences, provoking them to consider social and political realities that extend beyond the characters and events depicted onstage. Brecht’s influence can be seen in English playwright Caryl Churchill’s 1979 play Cloud 9: although the play sometimes invites empathetic reactions, it primarily works to engage audiences in an interrogation of patriarchy and colonialism, which it does by placing audiences at a distance, thereby encouraging them to ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: focus on the characters’ beliefs about social and political issues as revealed by the characters’ actions.
choices.B: reflect on social and political phenomena not directly related to patriarchy and colonialism.
choices.C: recognize pertinent social and political parallels between Germany during Brecht’s time and England at the time when Churchill was writing Cloud 9.
choices.D: be dispassionate as they think critically about the social and political questions raised by the play.

explanation: Brecht wanted intellectual rather than emotional engagement, and Churchill keeps audiences at a distance to make them interrogate patriarchy and colonialism. Distance plus critical thought is dispassion. B sends them to unrelated issues; the play aims them at its own.

passage.t: Archaeologists and historians used to believe that the Maya civilization during its Classic period (roughly 250–900) lacked agricultural marketplaces. One reason for this belief was that these scholars misunderstood the ecology of the regions the Maya inhabited. Marketplaces typically emerge because different individuals or groups want to trade resources they control for resources they don’t control. Scholars seriously underestimated the ecological diversity of the Maya landscape and thus assumed that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: marketplaces likely would not have attracted many traders from outside the regions controlled by the Maya.
choices.B: farming practices would have been largely the same throughout Maya lands even if the crops people produced varied significantly.
choices.C: marketplaces would not have enabled Maya people to acquire many products different from those they already produced.
choices.D: farmers would trade agricultural products only if they had already produced enough to meet their own needs.

explanation: Marketplaces arise when people want resources they don't control. Underrate the ecological diversity and you conclude everyone produced much the same things, leaving nothing worth trading for. A concerns outside traders rather than what locals could obtain.

passage.t: In a study of the mechanisms underlying associative memory—or the ability to learn and remember connections between inherently unrelated things—neuroscientists Kei Igarashi, Jasmine Chavez, and others presented mice with memory tests. The team discovered that fan cells, a type of cell found in the medial temporal lobe of the brain, are necessary for the acquisition of new associative memories. They also found that fan cell activity requires dopamine, a chemical the brain produces in response to pleasure and rewards. Consequently, receiving a reward should likely help to ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: decrease an individual’s capacity to utilize dopamine.
choices.B: increase an individual’s capacity to recognize differences between unrelated things.
choices.C: increase an individual’s capacity to form associative memories.
choices.D: decrease an individual’s capacity to create fan cells.

explanation: Fan cells are needed to acquire new associative memories, and fan cell activity requires dopamine, which the brain releases on reward. Chain those together and a reward should support forming associative memories. B substitutes recognising differences for associating things.

passage.t: Although military veterans make up a small proportion of the total population of the United States, they occupy a significantly higher proportion of the jobs in the civilian government. One possible explanation for this disproportionate representation is that military service familiarizes people with certain organizational structures that are also reflected in the civilian government bureaucracy, and this familiarity thus ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: makes civilian government jobs especially appealing to military veterans.
choices.B: alters the typical relationship between military service and subsequent career preferences.
choices.C: encourages nonveterans applying for civilian government jobs to consider military service instead.
choices.D: increases the number of civilian government jobs that require some amount of military experience to perform.

explanation: The explanation is that military service breeds familiarity with structures mirrored in government bureaucracy, and it has to account for veterans being overrepresented in those jobs. Familiarity drawing veterans toward the work does that. C reverses the direction entirely.

passage.t: Scientists studying Mars long thought the history of its crust was relatively simple. One reason for this is that geologic and climate data collected by a spacecraft showed that the crust was largely composed of basalt, likely as a result of intense volcanic activity that brought about a magma ocean, which then cooled to form the planet’s surface. A study led by Valerie Payré focused on additional information—further analysis of data collected by the spacecraft and infrared wavelengths detected from Mars’s surface—that revealed the presence of surprisingly high concentrations of silica in certain regions on Mars. Since a planetary surface that formed in a mostly basaltic environment would be unlikely to contain large amounts of silica, Payré concluded that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the information about silica concentrations collected by the spacecraft is likely more reliable than the silica information gleaned from infrared wavelengths detected from Mars’s surface.
choices.B: high silica concentrations on Mars likely formed from a different process than that which formed the crusts of other planets.
choices.C: having a clearer understanding of the composition of Mars’s crust and the processes by which it formed will provide more insight into how Earth’s crust formed.
choices.D: Mars’s crust likely formed as a result of other major geological events in addition to the cooling of a magma ocean.

explanation: High silica is unlikely to arise from a purely basaltic origin, yet silica is there. So the cooling magma ocean can't be the whole story — other processes must have shaped the crust too. A ranks the two data sources, which the text doesn't compare for reliability.

passage.t: Archaeologists have been debating the origin of a rare form of lead found in Shang dynasty (1766–1046 BCE) bronze artifacts since its presence was discovered in China in the 1990s. Different researchers have proposed theories on which regions of the world would have had the raw materials containing the specific lead in these artifacts, but no conclusive evidence has been presented. What is intriguing is that bronze artifacts from China dated after the Shang dynasty do not contain this form of lead, suggesting that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: Shang dynasty bronze pieces are rare and therefore more valuable than those from other time periods.
choices.B: the source of some of the raw materials used to make bronze was exploited only until the end of the Shang dynasty.
choices.C: bronze was used for a short time during the Shang dynasty before different metals were used to make artifacts.
choices.D: methods used to analyze bronze artifacts are not useful on pieces that are dated after the Shang dynasty.

explanation: The distinctive lead appears in Shang bronzes and not in later ones. The simplest account is that whatever supplied it stopped being used when the dynasty ended. C claims bronze itself was abandoned, but later bronze artifacts clearly exist.

passage.t: Herbivorous sauropod dinosaurs could grow more than 100 feet long and weigh up to 80 tons, and some researchers have attributed the evolution of sauropods to such massive sizes to increased plant production resulting from high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide during the Mesozoic era. However, there is no evidence of significant spikes in carbon dioxide levels coinciding with relevant periods in sauropod evolution, such as when the first large sauropods appeared, when several sauropod lineages underwent further evolution toward gigantism, or when sauropods reached their maximum known sizes, suggesting that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: fluctuations in atmospheric carbon dioxide affected different sauropod lineages differently.
choices.B: the evolution of larger body sizes in sauropods did not depend on increased atmospheric carbon dioxide.
choices.C: atmospheric carbon dioxide was higher when the largest known sauropods lived than it was when the first sauropods appeared.
choices.D: sauropods probably would not have evolved to such immense sizes if atmospheric carbon dioxide had been even slightly higher.

explanation: No carbon dioxide spikes line up with any of the three key moments in sauropod gigantism. If the proposed driver isn't present when the growth happens, the growth didn't depend on it. C asserts a difference in levels the evidence doesn't show.

passage.t: The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) is projected to maintain operation until at least 2030, but it has already revolutionized high-resolution imaging of solar-system bodies in visible and ultraviolet (UV) light wavelengths, notwithstanding that only about 6% of the bodies imaged by the HST are within the solar system. NASA researcher Cindy L. Young and colleagues assert that a new space telescope dedicated exclusively to solar-system observations would permit an extensive survey of minor solar-system bodies and long-term UV observation to discern how solar-system bodies change over time. Young and colleagues’ recommendation therefore implies that the HST ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: will likely continue to be used primarily to observe objects outside the solar system.
choices.B: will no longer be used to observe solar system objects if the telescope recommended by Young and colleagues is deployed.
choices.C: can be modified to observe the features of solar system objects that are of interest to Young and colleagues.
choices.D: lacks the sensors to observe the wavelengths of light needed to discern how solar system bodies change over time.

explanation: Only about 6% of the bodies HST has imaged are in our solar system, and the team wants a separate telescope precisely for solar-system work. That implies HST goes on doing what it mostly does — looking outward. D contradicts HST's established UV imaging.

passage.t: Geoglyphs are large-scale designs of lines or shapes created in a natural landscape. The Nazca Lines were created in the Nazca Desert in Peru by several Indigenous civilizations over a period of many centuries. Peruvian archaeologist Johny Isla specializes in these geoglyphs. At a German exhibit about the Nazca Lines, he saw an old photograph of a large geoglyph of a whalelike figure and was surprised that he didn’t recognize it. Isla returned to Peru and used a drone to search a wide area, looking for the figure from the air. This approach suggests that Isla thought that if he hadn’t already seen it, the whalelike geoglyph ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: must represent a species of whale that went extinct before there were any people in Peru.
choices.B: is actually located in Germany, not Peru, and isn’t part of the Nazca Lines at all.
choices.C: is probably in a location Isla hadn’t ever come across while on the ground.
choices.D: was almost certainly created a long time after the other Nazca Lines geoglyphs were created.

explanation: Isla knows these geoglyphs well and didn't recognise this one, so he searched a wide area by drone. Flying over ground he'd already walked makes sense only if he assumed it sat somewhere he'd never reached on foot.

passage.t: Some Astyanax mexicanus, a river-dwelling fish found in northeast Mexico, have colonized caves in the region. Although there is little genetic difference between river and cave A. mexicanus and all members of the species can emit the same sounds, biologist Carole Hyacinthe and colleagues found that the context and significance of those sounds vary by location—e.g., the click that river-dwelling A. mexicanus use to signal aggression is used by cave dwellers when foraging —and the acoustic properties of cave fish sounds show some cave-specific variations as well. Hyacinthe and colleagues note that differences in sonic communication could accumulate to the point of inhibiting interbreeding among fish from different locations, suggesting that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: although A. mexicanus living in rivers are genetically similar to those living in caves, river fish rely on sonic communication less than cave fish do.
choices.B: although A. mexicanus is a single species at present, it could be in the process of splitting into distinct populations with different characteristics.
choices.C: although all A. mexicanus emit sounds, the fish living in rivers produce some sounds that the fish living in caves do not, and vice versa.
choices.D: although A. mexicanus from different locations can interbreed currently, river fish and cave fish are sufficiently genetically distinct that they can be considered separate species.

explanation: Sound use already differs by location, and the researchers note those differences could eventually block interbreeding. That's a population in the early stages of dividing. D calls them separate species already, which the note about future divergence rules out.

passage.t: Dutch painters in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries often showed tables filled with large wheels of cheese or carved shards of butter. Some art historians, noting that dairy products were a major component of the Dutch diet, interpret these depictions as reflections of everyday Dutch eating habits. However, a group of researchers recently reviewed hundreds of food-related paintings and found that lemons—which could only be acquired in the Netherlands at great cost, since they had to be imported from warmer climates—feature in Dutch paintings of the period more than three times as frequently as dairy products do, thereby casting doubt on the idea that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: dairy products were a more significant component of the Dutch diet of the period than lemons were.
choices.B: food was a more popular subject among Dutch painters than it was among painters from other countries at the time.
choices.C: depictions of food in Dutch paintings of the period should be taken as realistic representations of Dutch eating habits.
choices.D: Dutch painters of the period may have depicted foods for symbolic reasons rather than to show what Dutch people typically ate.

explanation: Lemons were costly imports yet appear three times as often as dairy, which was a staple. So what's painted doesn't track what was eaten, undermining the realistic reading. A restates a fact the text accepts rather than the idea being doubted.

passage.t: Colonized by Spain in the 1600s, New Mexico is home to a dialect of Spanish that differs significantly from dialects spoken in Spain’s other former colonies in the Americas. Most notably, the New Mexican dialect retains older features of the language that other dialects lost in later centuries. But why would it have done so? New Mexico was so distant from population centers in Spain’s other colonies that it attracted few colonists after its initial colonization. Geographical isolation in turn would have limited the exposure of New Mexican colonists to changes occurring to Spanish grammar and vocabulary elsewhere in the empire. Thus, the present-day uniqueness of the New Mexican dialect suggests the extent to which ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a language can protect itself from being influenced by other languages.
choices.B: the grammar and vocabulary of any given language change from one generation to the next.
choices.C: geographical isolation can influence how a language develops.
choices.D: speakers of one dialect of a language can understand speakers of another dialect of that language.

explanation: Distance kept new colonists away, isolation kept New Mexican speakers from changes elsewhere, and the dialect kept old features as a result. The distinctiveness measures what isolation does to a language. A frames it as resistance to other languages, not to change within Spanish.

passage.t: Off-off-Broadway theaters emerged in the late 1950s as a rebellion against mainstream Broadway theaters in New York, freeing artists to create productions that were more experimental than typical Broadway shows. One such artist was playwright María Irene Fornés. Working with off-off Broadway theaters enabled Fornés not only to direct her own plays but also to direct them exactly as she intended them to be staged, regardless of how strange the results might have seemed to audiences accustomed to Broadway shows. In this way, Fornés ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: wrote plays that would have been too expensive to produce if someone else had directed the production.
choices.B: recognized that staging an off-off-Broadway play was more complicated than staging a Broadway play.
choices.C: would have been more famous if she had created plays that were mainstream instead of experimental.
choices.D: illustrates the artistic opportunity offered by off-off Broadway theaters.

explanation: Off-off-Broadway freed artists to be experimental, and Fornés used that freedom to direct her own plays exactly as she intended, however strange. She is the case that shows what those theaters made possible. C speculates about fame the text doesn't address.

passage.t: North American gray wolves usually have mixed gray and white fur, but some members of the species have a version of a gene, or gene variant, that gives them a mostly black coat instead. Sarah Cubaynes and her team studied twelve populations of North American gray wolves. They found that the black-furred wolves are more common in areas where outbreaks of distemper virus happen regularly. The team also discovered that the black-furred wolves are more likely to be immune to distemper than the gray-furred wolves are. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: North American gray wolves experience more outbreaks of distemper virus than other wolf species do.
choices.B: the gene variant that results in black fur may be linked to immunity to the distemper virus.
choices.C: the average life span of gray wolves is likely to increase over time because of a particular gene variant.
choices.D: gray-furred wolves will soon replace black-furred wolves across North America.

explanation: Black-furred wolves are commoner where distemper is common and are likelier to be immune to it. Taken together, the coat-colour variant looks tied to that immunity. D predicts a replacement the findings point away from.

passage.t: If some artifacts recovered from excavations of the settlement of Kuulo Kataa, in modern Ghana, date from the thirteenth century CE, that may lend credence to claims that the settlement was founded before or around that time. There is other evidence, however, strongly supporting a fourteenth century CE founding date for Kuulo Kataa. If both the artifact dates and the fourteenth century CE founding date are correct, that would imply that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: artifacts from the fourteenth century CE are more commonly recovered than are artifacts from the thirteenth century CE.
choices.B: the artifacts originated elsewhere and eventually reached Kuulo Kataa through trade or migration.
choices.C: Kuulo Kataa was founded by people from a different region than had previously been assumed.
choices.D: excavations at Kuulo Kataa may have inadvertently damaged some artifacts dating to the fourteenth century CE.

explanation: If the artifacts really are thirteenth-century but the settlement was founded in the fourteenth, they can't have been made there. They must have come from elsewhere and arrived later. C changes who founded it, which doesn't reconcile the dates.

passage.t: Indigenous cultures possess unique knowledge of the medicinal uses of plants. According to a 2021 study, 73 percent of the medicinal uses of plants native to North America are reflected in the vocabulary of a single Indigenous language. However, as more and more Indigenous people exclusively speak a globally dominant language, such as English, their ancestral languages fade from daily use. These facts lend added importance to tribal nations’ efforts to preserve their languages. By ensuring the continued use of Cherokee, Ojibwe, and the hundreds of other Indigenous languages in what is now the United States, tribal nations are also ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: increasing the number of medicinal plants represented in the vocabularies of Indigenous languages.
choices.B: transmitting terms for medicinal plants from Indigenous languages to globally dominant languages.
choices.C: preserving knowledge about the medicinal value of plants native to the tribal nations’ lands.
choices.D: ensuring that citizens of tribal nations have physical access to medicinal plants.

explanation: Most medicinal uses of native plants are encoded in a single Indigenous language, and those languages fade as speakers shift to dominant ones. Keeping the languages alive keeps that plant knowledge alive. A would mean adding new plants rather than retaining knowledge.

passage.t: When the Vinland Map, a map of the world purported to date to the mid-1400s, surfaced in 1957, some scholars believed it demonstrated that European knowledge of the eastern coast of present-day North America predated Christopher Columbus’s 1492 arrival. In 2021, a team including conservators Marie-France Lemay and Paula Zyats and materials scientist Anikó Bezur performed an extensive analysis of the map and the ink used. They found that the ink contains titanium dioxide, a compound that was first introduced in ink manufacturing in the early 1900s. Therefore, the team concluded that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: mid-1400s Europeans could not have known about the eastern coast of present-day North America.
choices.B: the Vinland Map could not have been drawn by mid-1400s mapmakers.
choices.C: mapmakers must have used titanium compounds in their ink in the 1400s.
choices.D: there isn’t enough information to determine when the ink was created.

explanation: The ink contains titanium dioxide, which entered ink manufacturing in the early 1900s. A mid-1400s mapmaker could not have used it, so the map is not from that period. A overreaches into what Europeans knew, which the ink says nothing about.

passage.t: It’s common for jazz musicians and fans to refer to certain songs as having “swing,” indicating that the songs provoke a strong feeling, like the impulse to tap one’s foot or dance. The exact acoustic properties that give a song swing, however, have long been thought to be undefinable. To investigate swing, a team led by physicist Corentin Nelias delayed the downbeats and synchronized the offbeats in jazz piano solos and asked jazz musicians to compare the intensity of swing in each modified piece with the intensity of swing in the original piece. They found that participants were more than seven times likelier to characterize the modified songs as having swing than to characterize the original versions as having swing, suggesting that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: synchronized offbeats tend to give a song swing regardless of whether downbeats are delayed.
choices.B: the acoustic properties that give a song swing are not easy for jazz musicians to manipulate.
choices.C: jazz songs that feature the piano are more likely to have swing than are jazz songs that do not feature the piano.
choices.D: the timing of downbeats and offbeats may play a crucial role in giving a song swing.

explanation: Delaying downbeats and synchronising offbeats made musicians over seven times likelier to hear swing. Changing the timing changed the perception, so timing is doing the work. A credits offbeats alone, but both were altered together.

passage.t: The Indus River valley civilization flourished in South Asia from 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE. Many examples of the civilization’s writing system exist, but researchers haven’t yet deciphered it or identified which ancient language it represents. Nevertheless, archaeologists have found historical artifacts, such as clay figures and jewelry, that provide information about the civilization’s customs and how its communities were organized. The archaeologists’ findings therefore suggest that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: investigating an ancient civilization is easier without knowledge of the civilization’s language.
choices.B: knowing an ancient civilization’s language isn’t necessary in order to learn details about the civilization.
choices.C: archaeological research should focus on finding additional artifacts rather than deciphering ancient languages.
choices.D: examining the civilization’s historical artifacts has resolved the debate about this civilization’s language.

explanation: The script is still undeciphered, yet figures and jewellery have revealed customs and social organisation. So real knowledge is possible without the language. A goes further and calls the absence an advantage.

passage.t: To investigate the history of plate subduction—when one of Earth’s tectonic plates slides beneath another—Sarah M. Aarons and colleagues compared ancient rocks from the Acasta Gneiss Complex in Canada to modern rocks. Using isotope analysis, the researchers found that Acasta rocks dating to about 4.02 billion years ago (bya) most strongly resemble modern rocks formed in a plume setting (an area in which hot rocks from Earth’s mantle flow upward into the crust). By contrast, they found that Acasta rocks dating to about 3.75 bya and 3.6 bya have an isotope composition that is similar to that of modern rocks formed in a subduction setting. Aarons’s team therefore concluded that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: subduction-like processes began occurring in some locations no later than 3.75 bya.
choices.B: subduction replaced mantle plume formation as the most common geological process by about 4.02 bya.
choices.C: the majority of the rocks in the Acasta Gneiss Complex formed through subduction.
choices.D: the rocks in the Acasta Gneiss Complex are of a more recent origin than scientists previously thought.

explanation: Rocks from 4.02 bya match plume settings, while those from 3.75 and 3.6 bya match subduction settings. The earliest subduction-like signature is the 3.75 bya rock, so such processes were under way by then. B has subduction dominant by 4.02 bya, before any such signature appears.

passage.t: Ratified by more than 90 countries, the Nagoya Protocol is an international agreement ensuring that Indigenous communities are compensated when their agricultural resources and knowledge of wild plants and animals are utilized by agricultural corporations. However, the protocol has shortcomings. For example, it allows corporations to insist that their agreements with communities to conduct research on the commercial uses of the communities’ resources and knowledge remain confidential. Therefore, some Indigenous advocates express concern that the protocol may have the unintended effect of ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: diminishing the monetary reward that corporations might derive from their agreements with Indigenous communities.
choices.B: limiting the research that corporations conduct on the resources of the Indigenous communities with which they have signed agreements.
choices.C: preventing independent observers from determining whether the agreements guarantee equitable compensation for Indigenous communities.
choices.D: discouraging Indigenous communities from learning new methods for harvesting plants and animals from their corporate partners.

explanation: Corporations can require the agreements stay confidential, so nobody outside can check whether the compensation is fair. That's the worry. A and B describe costs to corporations, not to the communities the protocol protects.

passage.t: Laura Mulvey has theorized that in narrative film, shots issuing from a protagonist’s point of view compel viewers to identify with the character. Such identification is heightened by “invisible editing,” or editing so inconspicuous that it renders cuts between shots almost unnoticeable. Conversely, Mulvey proposes that conspicuous editing or an absence of point-of-view shots would induce a more critical stance toward a protagonist. Consider, for example, the attic scene in Alfred Hitchcock’s The Birds, a conspicuously edited sequence of tens of shots, few of which correspond to the protagonist’s point of view. According to Mulvey’s logic, this scene should affect viewers by ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: obscuring their awareness of the high degree of artifice involved in constructing the montage.
choices.B: lessening their identification with the protagonist, if not alienating them from the character altogether.
choices.C: compelling them to identify with the film’s director, whose proxy is the camera, and not with the protagonist.
choices.D: diverting their attention away from the film’s content and toward its stylistic attributes.

explanation: Point-of-view shots plus invisible editing build identification; Mulvey says conspicuous editing and few point-of-view shots do the opposite. The attic scene has both, so identification should weaken. C substitutes identifying with the director.

passage.t: The increased integration of digital technologies throughout the process of book creation in the late 20th and early 21st centuries lowered the costs of book production, but those decreased costs have been most significant in the manufacturing and distribution process, which occurs after the authoring, editing, and design of the book are complete. This suggests that in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: digital technologies made it easier than it had been previously for authors to write very long works and get them published.
choices.B: customers generally expected the cost of books to decline relative to the cost of other consumer goods.
choices.C: publishers increased the variety of their offerings by printing more unique titles but also printed fewer copies of each title.
choices.D: the costs of writing, editing, and designing a book were less affected by the technologies used than were the costs of manufacturing and distributing a book.

explanation: Digital tools cut costs mainly in manufacturing and distribution, the stages after authoring, editing and design. So the earlier creative stages saw less benefit. B and C move to customer expectations and print runs, neither of which follows.

passage.t: Many animals, including humans, must sleep, and sleep is known to have a role in everything from healing injuries to encoding information in long-term memory. But some scientists claim that, from an evolutionary standpoint, deep sleep for hours at a time leaves an animal so vulnerable that the known benefits of sleeping seem insufficient to explain why it became so widespread in the animal kingdom. These scientists therefore imply that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: prolonged deep sleep is likely advantageous in ways that have yet to be discovered.
choices.B: most traits perform functions that are hard to understand from an evolutionary standpoint.
choices.C: it is more important to understand how widespread prolonged deep sleep is than to understand its function.
choices.D: many traits that provide significant benefits for an animal also likely pose risks to that animal.

explanation: Hours of vulnerability would be selected against unless something outweighed it, and the known benefits don't. If deep sleep spread anyway, there must be advantages not yet identified. D generalises to traits at large rather than resolving this puzzle.

passage.t: The Haitian Declaration of Independence was issued in 1804, bringing to an end the revolution against colonial France that began in 1791. Written in French, which was not the first language of most Haitians but which was used throughout Europe as the language of international diplomacy, the declaration notes that Haiti will not bring rebellion to other Caribbean nations, promises to respect the sovereignty of its neighbors—widely understood as a reassurance to the United States—and sets up Haiti as an example for future struggles against colonizers (an implicit reference to the many colonies then found in the Americas). So even though the declaration is explicitly addressed to the Haitian people, it’s reasonable to conclude that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: aspects of the declaration were modeled on similar documents from other countries.
choices.B: the French government may have been surprised by the declaration.
choices.C: many Haitian people opposed the revolution and the declaration.
choices.D: the declaration actually had several intended audiences.

explanation: Written in the language of diplomacy, reassuring neighbours, addressing the United States, and modelling resistance for other colonies — every feature reaches past Haiti. So the nominal address to Haitians isn't the whole story. B guesses at French reaction.

passage.t: Researchers Suchithra Rajendran and Maximilian Popfinger modeled varying levels of passenger redistribution from short-haul flights (flights of 50 to 210 minutes, from takeoff to landing) to high-speed rail trips. Planes travel faster than trains, but air travel typically requires 3 hours of lead time for security, baggage handling, and boarding that rail travel doesn’t, so short-haul routes take similar amounts of time by air and by rail. However, the model suggests that as rail passenger volumes approach current capacity limits, long lead times emerge. Therefore, for rail to remain a viable alternative to short-haul flights, ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: rail systems should offer fewer long-haul routes and airlines should offer more long-haul routes.
choices.B: rail systems may need to schedule additional trains for these routes.
choices.C: security, baggage handling, and boarding procedures used by airlines may need to be implemented for rail systems.
choices.D: passengers who travel by rail for these routes will need to accept that lead times will be similar to those for air travel.

explanation: Rail matches air on these routes only while lead times stay short, and lead times grow as trains approach capacity. Adding services is what keeps capacity ahead of demand. C would import the very delays that make air travel slow.

passage.t: Euphorbia esula (leafy spurge) is a Eurasian plant that has become invasive in North America, where it displaces native vegetation and sickens cattle. E. esula can be controlled with chemical herbicides, but that approach can also kill harmless plants nearby. Recent research on introducing engineered DNA into plant species to inhibit their reproduction may offer a path toward exclusively targeting E. esula, consequently ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: making individual E. esula plants more susceptible to existing chemical herbicides.
choices.B: enhancing the ecological benefits of E. esula in North America.
choices.C: enabling cattle to consume E. esula without becoming sick.
choices.D: reducing invasive E. esula numbers without harming other organisms.

explanation: Herbicides work but kill harmless neighbouring plants; engineered DNA could suppress reproduction in E. esula alone. The gain is control without collateral damage. B has the invasive plant becoming beneficial, which reverses the problem.

passage.t: Henry Ossawa Tanner’s 1893 painting The Banjo Lesson, which depicts an elderly man teaching a boy to play the banjo, is regarded as a landmark in the history of works by Black artists in the United States. Scholars should be cautious when ascribing political or ideological values to the painting, however: beliefs and assumptions that are commonly held now may have been unfamiliar to Tanner and his contemporaries, and vice versa. Scholars who forget this fact when discussing The Banjo Lesson therefore ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: risk judging Tanner’s painting by standards that may not be historically appropriate.
choices.B: tend to conflate Tanner’s political views with those of his contemporaries.
choices.C: forgo analyzing Tanner’s painting in favor of analyzing his political activity.
choices.D: wrongly assume that Tanner’s painting was intended as a critique of his fellow artists.

explanation: Present-day assumptions may have been foreign to Tanner and his contemporaries. Forget that and you read the painting through values that weren't available to it. B and D name specific errors the caution doesn't single out.

passage.t: In many cultures, a handshake can create trust between people. Engineer João Avelino and his team are designing a robot to shake hands with a human in order to improve human-robot interactions. The robot hand adjusts its movements and pressure to better imitate the feel of a human hand. The researchers want the robot’s handshake to feel realistic because ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: lifelike handshakes may make people more comfortable interacting with robots.
choices.B: it’s easier to program a robot to perform handshakes than it is to program a robot to perform some other types of greetings.
choices.C: people are less likely to interact with robots that don’t look like humans.
choices.D: the robot in the researchers’ study may have uses other than interacting with humans.

explanation: A handshake builds trust between people, and the team is refining the robot's grip to feel human. The point of realism is to make interacting with the robot easier to accept. B and D shift to programming ease and other uses.

passage.t: In a study of the cognitive abilities of white-faced capuchin monkeys (Cebus imitator), researchers neglected to control for the physical difficulty of the tasks they used to evaluate the monkeys. The cognitive abilities of monkeys given problems requiring little dexterity, such as sliding a panel to retrieve food, were judged by the same criteria as were those of monkeys given physically demanding problems, such as unscrewing a bottle and inserting a straw. The results of the study, therefore, ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: could suggest that there are differences in cognitive ability among the monkeys even though such differences may not actually exist.
choices.B: are useful for identifying tasks that the monkeys lack the cognitive capacity to perform but not for identifying tasks that the monkeys can perform.
choices.C: should not be taken as indicative of the cognitive abilities of any monkey species other than C. imitator.
choices.D: reveal more about the monkeys’ cognitive abilities when solving artificial problems than when solving problems encountered in the wild.

explanation: Monkeys facing easy tasks and monkeys facing dexterity-heavy ones were judged by the same standard, so a poor result may reflect the physical demand rather than the thinking. The study can manufacture differences that aren't cognitive.

passage.t: A team of biologists led by Jae-Hoon Jung, Antonio D. Barbosa, and Stephanie Hutin investigated the mechanism that allows Arabidopsis thaliana (thale cress) plants to accelerate flowering at high temperatures. They replaced the protein ELF3 in the plants with a similar protein found in another species (stiff brome) that, unlike A. thaliana, displays no acceleration in flowering with increased temperature. A comparison of unmodified A. thaliana plants with the altered plants showed no difference in flowering at 22° Celsius, but at 27° Celsius, the unmodified plants exhibited accelerated flowering while the altered ones did not, which suggests that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: temperature-sensitive accelerated flowering is unique to A. thaliana.
choices.B: A. thaliana increases ELF3 production as temperatures rise.
choices.C: ELF3 enables A. thaliana to respond to increased temperatures.
choices.D: temperatures of at least 22° Celsius are required for A. thaliana to flower.

explanation: Swapping in the stiff brome protein changed nothing at 22°C but removed the acceleration at 27°C. The one altered component is therefore what carries the heat response. B claims more ELF3 is produced, which the swap doesn't test.

passage.t: A heliograph is a semaphore device used for sending optical communications—usually in the form of Morse code—by reflecting flashes of sunlight off a mirror. Heliographs were used for rapid communication across expansive distances for military, surveying, and forestry purposes during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, but they were largely effective only during the daytime, and the range of the device depended on factors such as the opacity of the air and line of sight. Therefore, heliographs were eventually replaced by technology that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: worked on similar principles but was easier to produce and maintain.
choices.B: was not so constrained by environmental circumstances.
choices.C: could be used for more than military, surveying, or forestry purposes.
choices.D: enabled communication that didn’t require knowledge of Morse code.

explanation: Heliographs needed daylight, clear air and line of sight — all conditions of the environment. A replacement worth adopting would be free of those limits. A keeps the same principles and so the same constraints.

passage.t: Martin Dančák, Wewin Tjiasmanto, and colleagues have identified a new carnivorous plant species (Nepenthes pudica) in Indonesia. Like other carnivorous plants, N. pudica has pitfall traps, or pitchers, that capture prey, but unlike others, the pitchers of N. pudica are located underground. The researchers unearthed the new species on fairly dry ridges with surfaces that host few other plants and animals. Therefore, the researchers hypothesize that the N. pudica species likely ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: represents one of many undiscovered carnivorous plant species in the region.
choices.B: formed pitchers early in development to absorb more moisture.
choices.C: is buried by nearby animals as they forage along the ridges for food.
choices.D: evolved to have underground traps to access more prey than would surface traps.

explanation: The pitchers are underground, and the ridges where the plant grows have surfaces hosting few animals. If prey is scarce above and available below, burying the traps is the point. B swaps prey capture for absorbing moisture.

passage.t: By running computer simulations of the development of our solar system, André Izidoro, Rajdeep Dasgupta, and colleagues concluded that the Sun may have been surrounded by three giant dust rings before the planets started to form. The researchers suggest that the materials in the innermost ring became the four planets closest to the Sun, the materials in the middle ring produced the rest of the planets, and the materials in the outermost ring created the asteroids and other small bodies in the region beyond Neptune. In one simulation, the researchers delayed the initial formation of the middle ring, causing oversized super-Earths to begin developing from the innermost ring. The researchers therefore hypothesize that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the middle ring formed earlier in the solar system’s development than the initial simulations suggested.
choices.B: the timing of the initial formation of the middle ring played an important role in determining the eventual size of Earth.
choices.C: if the formation of the outermost ring had occurred earlier in a simulation, all the planets would have become super- Earths.
choices.D: the innermost ring actually formed into all the planets in our solar system, not just the four closest to the Sun.

explanation: Delaying the middle ring caused super-Earths to form from the innermost ring, which is where Earth comes from. When that ring formed therefore shaped how big Earth ended up. C moves to the outermost ring, which wasn't the variable changed.

passage.t: Ancestral Puebloans, the civilization from which present-day Pueblo tribes descended, emerged as early as 1500 B.C.E. in an area of what is now the southwestern United States and dispersed suddenly in the late 1200s C.E., abandoning established villages with systems for farming crops and turkeys. Recent analysis comparing turkey remains at Mesa Verde, one such village in southern Colorado, to samples from modern turkey populations in the Rio Grande Valley of north central New Mexico determined that the latter birds descended in part from turkeys cultivated at Mesa Verde, with shared genetic markers appearing only after 1280. Thus, researchers concluded that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: conditions of the terrains in the Rio Grande Valley and Mesa Verde had greater similarities in the past than they do today.
choices.B: some Ancestral Puebloans migrated to the Rio Grande Valley in the late 1200s and carried farming practices with them.
choices.C: Indigenous peoples living in the Rio Grande Valley primarily planted crops and did not cultivate turkeys before 1280.
choices.D: the Ancestral Puebloans of Mesa Verde likely adopted the farming practices of Indigenous peoples living in other regions.

explanation: Rio Grande turkeys descend partly from Mesa Verde stock, with shared markers appearing only after 1280 — exactly when Mesa Verde was abandoned. People moved north and brought their birds and practices. D reverses who adopted from whom.

passage.t: Birds of many species ingest foods containing carotenoids, pigmented molecules that are converted into feather coloration. Coloration tends to be especially saturated in male birds’ feathers, and because carotenoids also confer health benefits, the deeply saturated colors generally serve to communicate what is known as an honest signal of a bird’s overall fitness to potential mates. However, ornithologist Allison J. Shultz and others have found that males in several species of the tanager genus Ramphocelus use microstructures in their feathers to manipulate light, creating the appearance of deeper saturation without the birds necessarily having to maintain a carotenoid-rich diet. These findings suggest that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: individual male tanagers can engage in honest signaling without relying on carotenoid consumption.
choices.B: feather microstructures may be less effective than deeply saturated feathers for signaling overall fitness.
choices.C: scientists have yet to determine why tanagers have a preference for mates with colorful appearances.
choices.D: a male tanager’s appearance may function as a dishonest signal of the individual’s overall fitness.

explanation: Saturated colour normally signals a carotenoid-rich diet and good health. These tanagers produce the look structurally, without the diet, so the display can overstate fitness. A calls that honest signalling, which is what the microstructures bypass.

passage.t: Among social animals that care for their young, such as chickens, macaque monkeys, and humans, newborns appear to show an innate attraction to faces and face-like stimuli. Elisabetta Versace and her colleagues used an image of three black dots arranged in the shape of eyes and a nose or mouth to test whether this trait also occurs in Testudo tortoises, which live alone and do not engage in parental care. They found that tortoise hatchlings showed a significant preference for the image, suggesting that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: face-like stimuli are likely perceived as harmless by newborns of social species that practice parental care but as threatening by newborns of solitary species without parental care.
choices.B: researchers should not assume that an innate attraction to face-like stimuli is necessarily an adaptation related to social interaction or parental care.
choices.C: researchers can assume that the attraction to face-like stimuli that is seen in social species that practice parental care is learned rather than innate.
choices.D: newly hatched Testudo tortoises show a stronger preference for face-like stimuli than adult Testudo tortoises do.

explanation: Tortoises live alone and give no parental care, yet hatchlings still prefer face-like patterns. So the preference can exist without any social explanation, and shouldn't be assumed to be one. C calls the trait learned, which hatchlings rule out.

passage.t: Aerogels are highly porous foams consisting mainly of tiny air pockets within a solidified gel. These lightweight materials are often applied to spacecraft and other equipment required to withstand extreme conditions, as they provide excellent insulation despite typically being brittle and eventually fracturing due to degradation from repeated exposure to high heat. Now, Xiangfeng Duan of the University of California, Los Angeles, and colleagues have developed an aerogel with uniquely flexible properties. Unlike earlier aerogels, Duan’s team’s material contracts rather than expands when heated and fully recovers after compressing to just 5% of its original volume, suggesting that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the aerogel’s remarkable flexibility results from its higher proportion of air pockets to solidified gel as compared to other aerogels.
choices.B: the aerogel’s overall strength is greater than that of other insulators but its ability to withstand exposure to intense heat is lower.
choices.C: the aerogel will be more effective as an insulator for uses that involve gradual temperature shifts than for those that involve rapid heat increases.
choices.D: the aerogel will be less prone to the structural weakness that ultimately causes most other aerogels to break down with use.

explanation: Ordinary aerogels expand with heat and fracture from repeated exposure; this one contracts instead and recovers fully after severe compression. Those are the properties whose absence caused the breakdown. B claims worse heat tolerance, the opposite of the point.

passage.t: In the South Pacific, New Caledonian crows use two different kinds of stick tools. One tool is complex. The crows shape a stick from a rare plant into a hook. The other tool is basic. The crows find a stick without a hook on the ground. The hooked tool is harder to get but is much better than the basic tool at removing prey from holes. When studying New Caledonian crows, ecologist Barbara Klump found that they hold the hooked tools in their claws when not using them, or they carefully put them in a safe place. The crows don’t do the same with the basic tools. This suggests to Klump that the ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: hooked stick tools are more valuable to the crows than the stick tools without hooks.
choices.B: hooked stick tools are easier for most of the crows to hold than the stick tools without hooks.
choices.C: crows prefer to share their hooked stick tools but don’t share the stick tools without hooks.
choices.D: crows realize that both kinds of stick tools are less effective than their claws are at removing prey from holes.

explanation: Hooked tools are hard to make and far better at extracting prey, and the crows keep them underfoot or stow them safely while leaving basic sticks lying about. Guarding one and not the other tracks what each is worth.

passage.t: In documents called judicial opinions, judges explain the reasoning behind their legal rulings, and in those explanations they sometimes cite and discuss historical and contemporary philosophers. Legal scholar and philosopher Anita L. Allen argues that while judges are naturally inclined to mention philosophers whose views align with their own positions, the strongest judicial opinions consider and rebut potential objections; discussing philosophers whose views conflict with judges’ views could therefore ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: allow judges to craft judicial opinions without needing to consult philosophical works.
choices.B: help judges improve the arguments they put forward in their judicial opinions.
choices.C: make judicial opinions more comprehensible to readers without legal or philosophical training.
choices.D: bring judicial opinions in line with views that are broadly held among philosophers.

explanation: Judges gravitate to philosophers who agree with them, but the strongest opinions anticipate and answer objections. Engaging opposing philosophers is how that happens, so it strengthens the argument. C and D shift to readability and consensus.

passage.t: Georgia Douglas Johnson wrote many plays in the 1920s and 1930s. At the time, professional theater companies rarely put on plays by Black women, so few of Johnson’s plays made it to the stage. Only a small number of her plays were published in her lifetime. But that doesn’t mean that Johnson never learned what other people thought of her plays.

Johnson hosted weekly get-togethers for fellow Black writers and artists in her Washington, D.C., home. Attendees would read and discuss one another’s work, including Johnson’s own. These gatherings could therefore serve as ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: an occasion for professional theater companies to put on plays.
choices.B: an opportunity for Johnson to get feedback on her plays.
choices.C: a way for Johnson to learn about plays that were produced in other cities.
choices.D: subject matter for future plays by Johnson.

explanation: Few of Johnson's plays were staged or published, yet the text insists she still learned what others thought. The weekly gatherings, where writers read and discussed one another's work including hers, are how. A stages plays the passage says rarely happened.

passage.t: Many mosquito repellents contain natural components that work by activating multiple odor receptors on mosquitoes’ antennae. As the insects develop resistance, new repellents are needed. Ke Dong and her team found that EBF, a molecular component of a chrysanthemum-flower extract, can repel mosquitoes by activating just one odor receptor— and this receptor, Or31, is present in all mosquito species known to carry diseases. Therefore, the researchers suggest that in developing new repellents, it would be most useful to ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: identify molecular components similar to EBF that target the activation of Or31 receptors.
choices.B: investigate alternative methods for extracting EBF molecules from chrysanthemums.
choices.C: verify the precise locations of Or31 and other odor receptors on mosquitoes’ antennae.
choices.D: determine the maximum number of different odor receptors that can be activated by a single molecule.

explanation: EBF repels by activating Or31 alone, and Or31 is present in every disease-carrying mosquito species. The obvious next step is to look for other molecules that hit that same receptor. D chases the opposite property — activating many receptors at once.

passage.t: Alice Guy-Blaché directed hundreds of films between 1896 and 1920. She wanted audiences to feel like they were watching real people on screen. She would encourage actors in her films to behave naturally. Guy-Blaché even hung a large sign reading “Be Natural” in the studio where she made her films. At the time, films lacked sound, so actors needed to rely solely on their bodies and facial expressions to convey emotions. As a result, actors tended to highly exaggerate their actions and expressions. The style of acting in Guy-Blaché’s films was therefore ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: copied by many of Guy-Blaché’s peers.
choices.B: familiar to actors who had worked on other directors’ films.
choices.C: very unusual for the period.
choices.D: better than film acting today.

explanation: Silent film pushed actors toward highly exaggerated gestures, and Guy-Blaché told hers to be natural, even hanging a sign. Against that backdrop her style was the exception. A and B would make it typical, which the contrast denies.

passage.t: Volunteering, or giving time for a community service for free, is a valuable form of civic engagement because helping in a community is also good for society as a whole. In a survey of youths in the United States, most young people said that they believe volunteering is a way to help people on an individual level. Meanwhile, only 6% of the youths said that they think volunteering is a way to help fix problems in society overall. These replies suggest that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: many young people think they can volunteer only within their own communities.
choices.B: volunteering may be even more helpful than many young people think it is.
choices.C: volunteering can help society overall more than it can help individual people.
choices.D: many young people may not know how to find ways to volunteer their time.

explanation: Young people mostly see volunteering as helping individuals, and only 6% see it as addressing problems in society — yet the opening states it does benefit society as a whole. The gap is between the real benefit and their view of it.

passage.t: Tides can deposit large quantities of dead vegetation within a salt marsh, smothering healthy plants and leaving a salt panne—a depression devoid of plants that tends to trap standing water—in the marsh’s interior. Ecologist Kathryn Beheshti and colleagues found that burrowing crabs living within these pannes improve drainage by loosening the soil, leading the pannes to shrink as marsh plants move back in. At salt marsh edges, however, crab-induced soil loosening can promote marsh loss by accelerating erosion, suggesting that the burrowing action of crabs ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: can be beneficial to marshes with small pannes but can be harmful to marshes with large pannes.
choices.B: may promote increases in marsh plants or decreases in marsh plants, depending on the crabs’ location.
choices.C: tends to be more heavily concentrated in areas of marsh interiors with standing water than at marsh edges.
choices.D: varies in intensity depending on the size of the panne relative to the size of the surrounding marsh.

explanation: In pannes, burrowing crabs drain the soil and plants return; at marsh edges, the same loosening speeds erosion and marsh is lost. Identical behaviour, opposite outcomes, depending on where the crabs are. A makes panne size the variable rather than position.

passage.t: To create the poems in her 2017 collection One Last Word, poet Nikki Grimes used a writing method called the golden shovel. This method often involves choosing a line from an existing poem and then using each word from that line as the last word of each line in a new poem. Grimes wanted the poems in One Last Word to honor important Black poets of the past, so she chose lines by poets such as Langston Hughes and Georgia Douglas Johnson. Writing in this way can be challenging and might seem as though it would produce awkward poems. However, reviewers praised One Last Word as a beautiful and powerful tribute to the poets who inspired it. This reaction suggests that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: most reviewers didn’t understand Grimes’s goal for One Last Word.
choices.B: Grimes successfully used the golden shovel method to achieve her goal for One Last Word.
choices.C: Langston Hughes and Georgia Douglas Johnson are two of Grimes’s favorite poets.
choices.D: Grimes inspired many other writers to create poems using the golden shovel method.

explanation: Grimes chose the golden shovel to honour earlier Black poets, and reviewers called the result a beautiful and powerful tribute — despite the method's potential for awkwardness. The goal was met. A dismisses reviewers who clearly grasped the aim.

passage.t: Astronomers investigated the Arabia Terra region of Mars because it appears to contain irregularly shaped craters that may have been caused by massive volcanic explosions. In their investigations of Arabia Terra, the researchers found remnants of ash deposits in an amount and thickness that would result from a massive volcanic eruption. However, erosion and past resurfacing events could have modified the surface of the planet. Therefore, ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the current makeup of the Arabia Terra region might not accurately reflect the volcanic activity of Mars’s past.
choices.B: eruptions from Mars’s volcanoes were likely not as massive as astronomers previously believed.
choices.C: ash was most likely expelled from multiple different volcanoes on Mars’s surface.
choices.D: the craters found in the Arabia Terra region were necessarily created by events other than volcanic eruptions.

explanation: The ash deposits fit a massive eruption, but erosion and resurfacing could since have altered the surface. So what's visible now may not faithfully record the volcanic past. D denies volcanic origin entirely, which the ash evidence supports.

passage.t: The ancient Sumerian civilization formed around 4000 BCE between two large rivers in an area that is now Iraq and Syria. The extremely hot and sunny weather in that area helped crops grow very quickly, but it also made it hard to keep the crops from drying up and dying. So, the Sumerians used water from the rivers in their farming. That method worked so well that they often could harvest even more crops than they needed in a season. As a result, the Sumerians ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: harvested crops only on the hottest days of each season.
choices.B: found ways to shield their crops from the sun.
choices.C: did not begin farming until long after 4000 BCE.
choices.D: were able to store extra crops for later use.

explanation: River water let the Sumerians harvest more than they needed in a season. A surplus has to go somewhere, and keeping it for later is what follows. B addresses the sun problem that irrigation already solved.

passage.t: Compiled in the late 1500s largely through the efforts of Indigenous scribes, Cantares Mexicanos is the most important collection of poetry in Classical Nahuatl, the principal language of the Aztec Empire. The poems portray Aztec society before the occupation of the empire by the army of Spain, and marginal notes in Cantares Mexicanos indicate that much of the collection’s content predates the initial invasion. Nonetheless, some of the poems contain inarguable references to beliefs and customs common in Spain during this era. Thus, some scholars have concluded that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: while its content largely predates the invasion, Cantares Mexicanos also contains additions made after the invasion.
choices.B: although those who compiled Cantares Mexicanos were fluent in Nahuatl, they had limited knowledge of the Spanish language.
choices.C: before the invasion by Spain, the poets of the Aztec Empire borrowed from the literary traditions of other societies.
choices.D: the references to beliefs and customs in Spain should be attributed to a coincidental resemblance between the societies of Spain and the Aztec Empire.

explanation: Marginal notes place most of the content before the invasion, yet some poems clearly reference Spanish beliefs and customs. Both can hold if material was added afterward. D dismisses those references as coincidence, which the text calls inarguable.

passage.t: “Gestures” in painting are typically thought of as bold, expressive brushstrokes. In the 1970s, American painter Jack Whitten built a 12-foot (3.7-meter) tool he named the “developer” to apply paint to an entire canvas in one motion, resulting in his series of “slab” paintings from that decade. Whitten described this process as making an entire painting in “one gesture,” signaling a clear departure from the prevalence of gestures in his work from the 1960s. Some art historians claim this shift represents “removing gesture” from the process. Therefore, regardless of whether using the developer constitutes a gesture, both Whitten and these art historians likely agree that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: any tool that a painter uses to create an artwork is capable of creating gestures.
choices.B: Whitten’s work from the 1960s exhibits many more gestures than his work from the 1970s does.
choices.C: Whitten became less interested in exploring the role of gesture in his work as his career progressed.
choices.D: Whitten’s work from the 1960s is much more realistic than his work from the 1970s is.

explanation: Whitten calls the developer “one gesture” and a departure from the 1960s work; the historians call it removing gesture. Either way, the earlier decade had many more. C and D go to his interests and realism, which neither side addresses.

passage.t: Researchers wanted to study how consumers’ reactions to an ad may be affected by other ads. The researchers began by showing study participants an ad for a product, with some seeing a less detailed ad and others seeing a more detailed one. Then, all participants viewed the same second ad for a store and shared their opinion of the store based on this second ad. Participants who had first seen an ad less detailed than the second ad had a higher opinion of the store than the participants who had first seen a more detailed ad. The researchers concluded that reactions to an ad may be affected by ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the number of people who viewed the ad.
choices.B: the length of time viewing previous ads.
choices.C: the amount of detail viewed in previous ads.
choices.D: the time of day that the ad is viewed.

explanation: The only thing varied was how detailed the first ad was, and opinions of the store shifted accordingly. So the detail level of a previous ad is what moved the reaction. B changes it to viewing time, which was held constant.

passage.t: As the name suggests, dramaturges originated in theater, where they continue to serve a variety of functions: conducting historical research for directors, compiling character biographies for actors, and perhaps most importantly, helping writers of plays and musicals to hone the works’ stories and characters. Performance scholar Susan Manning observes that many choreographers, like playwrights and musical theater writers, are concerned with storytelling and characterization. In fact, some choreographers describe the dances they create as expressions of narrative through movement; it is therefore unsurprising that ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: dramaturges can have a profound impact on the artistic direction of plays and musicals.
choices.B: choreographers developing dances with narrative elements frequently engage dramaturges to assist in refining those elements.
choices.C: dances by choreographers who incorporate narrative elements are more accessible to audiences than dances by choreographers who do not.
choices.D: some directors and actors rely too heavily on dramaturges to complete certain research tasks.

explanation: Dramaturges chiefly help writers refine story and character, and choreographers who describe dances as narrative are doing the same kind of work. Hiring them follows naturally. A restates their theatre role without making the connection to dance.

passage.t: Several artworks found among the ruins of the ancient Roman city of Pompeii depict a female figure fishing with a cupid nearby. Some scholars have asserted that the figure is the goddess Venus, since she is known to have been linked with cupids in Roman culture, but University of Leicester archaeologist Carla Brain suggests that cupids may have also been associated with fishing generally. The fact that a cupid is shown near the female figure, therefore, ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: is not conclusive evidence that the figure is Venus.
choices.B: suggests that Venus was often depicted fishing.
choices.C: eliminates the possibility that the figure is Venus.
choices.D: would be difficult to account for if the figure is not Venus.

explanation: The Venus reading rests on cupids being linked to her, but Brain notes cupids may have been associated with fishing generally. If so, the cupid could be there for the fishing, so it doesn't settle the identification. C overstates this into ruling Venus out.

passage.t: During the Bourbon Restoration in France (1814–1830), the right to vote required in part that a person paid at least 300 francs in direct taxes to the government. The four most common taxes (the quatre vieilles) were levied on real estate (both land and buildings); the doors and windows in taxpayer homes; the rental values of homes; and the businesses of artisans and merchants. (Foreign investments were either exempt from taxation or taxed lightly.) Although relatively few people paid the tax on real estate, it was the main means of voter qualification and accounted for over two-thirds of government receipts during this period, suggesting that during the Bourbon Restoration ______

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: those people who had the right to vote most likely had substantial holdings of French real estate.
choices.B: the voting habits of French artisans and merchants were effective in reducing tax burdens on businesses.
choices.C: the number of doors and windows in French residences was kept to a minimum but increased after 1830.
choices.D: French people with significant foreign investments were unlikely to have the right to vote.
